description: We’re looking for someone with coding experience (if you don’t, then that’s okay, as long as you dare to do something new and willing to learn).
summary: We developed Olympus Mons Navigator 3D, a health-first mission tool that keeps astronauts safe on a 572 km traverse from the plains to the summit caldera of Olympus Mons. Using NASA data, including Curiosity RAD radiation measurements, MOLA elevation and the USGS geologic map, it maps the health risks along the route: high radiation, extreme cold, steep slopes and toxic fine dust. For each risk it tells astronauts what to do. It tracks radiation dose against NASA limits, monitors oxygen and vital signs, and marks the point of no return. Random solar and dust storms trigger a shelter protocol inspired by NASA’s Artemis II, from early warning to a 72-hour symptom watch. Route planning and science stops are built around these safety limits. This addresses the challenge’s first priority, astronaut safety, on a hyperlocal Marswalk. It matters because astronauts facing a 4–24 minute signal delay must protect their own health on the spot, and this tool gives them the information to do so.
details: Olympus Mons Navigator 3D is an interactive 3D mission tool that helps a two-person crew plan and carry out a 572 km traverse from the plains northwest of Olympus Mons to its summit caldera. The crew does science along the way, and astronaut health is always the first priority. It works by layering NASA and USGS data on a 3.7 km grid: MOLA elevation and slope, the USGS SIM 3292 geologic map, a Viking mosaic from JPL Mars Trek, modelled surface temperature and a radiation model calibrated with Curiosity RAD measurements. An A* search then compares a shortest and an optimal route, and the mission is simulated hour by hour, tracking oxygen, fuel, radiation dose and the point of no return. Along the route, the tool warns the crew about health-risk zones and random solar and dust storms, with clear shelter steps inspired by NASA’s Artemis II approach. It also shows animated astronauts doing field science at each geologic unit. The tool saves time by planning routes and stops ahead, uses oxygen, fuel and dose budgets effectively, keeps crews safer, and is easy to use because everything runs in a single offline HTML file in any browser. Its intended impact is to show how NASA’s rich data can become a hyperlocal, time-based plan. A crew facing a 4–24 minute signal delay could use it on the spot, and planners and students could use it to see how real data supports human exploration; the same pipeline can be reused for other sites. We built it on standard laptops, using Python and NumPy for the data pipeline and routing, FastAPI as an optional backend, JavaScript with three.js (WebGL) for real-time 3D, Blender for renders and the Web Audio API for sound. Claude (Anthropic) was used for data analysis and interpretation, for coding, debugging and troubleshooting, and for presentation, video and audio; the team defined the concept, made the design decisions and verified the results. The project is creative because it turns static maps into a “living” mission in which resources, health and random storms change on every run, and science is shown happening at the work site rather than just listed. Our team considered astronaut safety, rover and suit mobility, science value, usability for first-time users, and honesty about which values are measured and which are modelled.
